July 30, 2007

ALLEN, J.

[
1
]

How does it happen that a husband who provides superb parenting
to his two daughters in a supervised environment loses his access during a 37
day trial, and, by the end of the trial, is facing a claim to terminate his
access entirely?

[
2
]

The question of what, if any, access the husband should have is
but one of the issues in the trial.  There are many other issues to be
determined including:

•

whether the court should impose joint custody or grant the wife
sole custody of the two children;

•

whether, if access is terminated, there should be telephone
contact between the husband and the children;

•

whether either or both parents should be prevented from removing
the children from the province of Manitoba;

•

whether the husband’s passport should be held by some trusted
third party during visits;

•

whether to continue a prevention order under
The
Domestic
Violence and Stalking Act
, C.C.S.M. c. D93 (the “
DVSA
”)
that prohibits contact between the husband and the wife, the children and the
wife’s parents; restricts the husband’s ability to attend a local cultural
centre where the children attend school; restricts his right to access court
files; and restricts his access to the children’s school, medical and
psychological records;

•

whether the husband’s future access to the courts with regard to
this domestic file should be limited in some way;

•

whether the parties’ pre-nuptial agreement is valid, and if not,
whether certain of the wife’s assets, including a family trust, are shareable;

•

whether there is any property, jointly owned or otherwise, which
should be the subject of a reference to the Master for an accounting under
The

Family Property Act
;
R.S.M. 1987, c. M45
– Cap. F25 or any other
statute;

•

whether the husband is entitled to spousal support and if so, in
what amount and for what duration;

•

whether it is reasonable, pursuant to Sec 11(1)(b) of the
Divorce
Act,
R.S., 1985, c.3 (2
nd
Supp.) to grant the divorce given
that the wife is not seeking child support; and

•

the wife’s claim for solicitor and client costs.

BACKGROUND

[
3
]

The wife is from Winnipeg.  In 1992 she moved to Israel to
study.  There, she met the husband, an Israeli law student.  In 1994 they
became engaged and the wife decided to take out Israeli citizenship.  The
parties got married in Winnipeg on August 20, 1995.  At that time, the husband
was completing his articling year with a firm in Tel Aviv.

[
4
]

The wife’s family is wealthy.  The wife was the sole beneficiary
of a family trust.  When she assumed residency in Israel, and prior to the
marriage, her accountants moved her family trust from Canada to the Grand
Cayman Islands for tax purposes.

[
5
]

Prior to the marriage, the trust purchased an expensive home in
Israel.  It was expected that the house would be a home for the parties and an
investment for the trust.  Before the marriage, the wife also had her Israeli
lawyers prepare a pre-nuptial agreement.  While the husband objected to the
agreement, it was signed in Winnipeg five days before the marriage.

[
6
]

After the marriage, the parties returned to Israel where both
continued working.  Their first child was born in 1999 and their second in
2000.

[
7
]

After the first child was born, the husband’s behaviour began
deteriorating.  The wife consulted a lawyer who wrote to the husband.  Things
improved before the second daughter was born.

[
8
]

During this time frame, the husband qualified as a lawyer.  He
was employed by several different firms for various periods.  He also had
periods of unemployment.  The wife continued with her same employer, earning
about US$4,000 per month.

[
9
]

In the spring of 2002, the husband was again unemployed.  The
wife and children were in Canada for a visit when there was a terrorist attack
on a hotel very near the husband’s parents’ home.  He called the wife and
suggested they move to Canada.  They discussed logistics.  The husband made
inquiries about the immigration process.

[
10
]

The parties differ about whether the move was to be permanent or
for a few years, but the preparations included leasing the house, packing up
the household and making immigration inquiries.  The wife was able to keep her
employment on a contract basis.  In Winnipeg, the wife’s parents found them a
home to rent and enrolled the children in a daycare at the Asper Jewish
Community Campus.

[
11
]

The family arrived in Winnipeg in October 2002.  The husband
arrived on a tourist visa and within a month of arrival had applied for
permanent residence status.  In the meantime he was not allowed to work.  The
children attended daycare and the wife continued her job.

[
12
]

Despite the well meaning efforts of family and friends, the
husband did not adapt well to life in Canada.  He spent much of his free time
at the Asper Campus, a community centre for Jewish culture.  He resented his
father-in-law and stopped participating in family life.  He had angry outbursts
and would get agitated very quickly.  He took out his frustrations about the
wife and her family on the children, saying cruel things to them about their
mother and grandparents.  After an incident where he threw water and a shirt at
the wife, she decided that the marriage was over.

[
13
]

The wife planned the separation in advance.  She consulted her
accountants and lawyers.  Before she told the husband about the separation, the
court papers were prepared and ready to be served.  She arranged for the
children to be at their grandparents and had her father wait in the driveway
when she told the husband that she was leaving.

[
14
]

The husband was very upset.  The wife told him he had to leave
the home but she would help him find an apartment.  She said she had left half
of the money in their joint account for him.  She told him he could continue to
use their leased car.  She said she and the children would be at her parents
until he had a plan.  She showed him the separation papers, including a draft
court order.  She drove him to her lawyer’s office so he could be served the
court documents but when they arrived, he refused to go into the law office.
When she returned to her parents’ home, he called dozens of times, came over
and refused to leave the doorstep for some time.  He was upset and crying.

[
15
]

Late the next day, the husband showed up unannounced at the
lawyer’s office.  He signed the consent order giving the wife sole custody with
access to be agreed.  He agreed to leave the house within a few days and the
order contained that term as well.

[
16
]

For a few weeks, the husband lived at a motel.  His father-in-law
then found him an apartment.  He was given a cell phone.  His immigration
status did not allow him to work.  His only means of support was about $7,500
in the couple’s joint account.  He was expected to pay his rent, the car lease
and cell phone bills from these funds until his work permit came through.

[
17
]

The wife allowed him to see the children twice a week.  The
visits were often problematic as he would not leave at the end of a visit
without a fuss, or would bring the children back early.  He made insulting
comments about the wife and her parents in front of the children.  He often
took the children to the Asper Campus where apparently other members began
making negative comments about his behaviour.  He also spent time at the
children’s daycare which the daycare found problematic as a result of his
inability to follow the rules and his tendency to exhibit impulsive behaviour.

[
18
]

About six weeks post-separation, the husband’s work permit
arrived.  He was only able to find minimum wage part time employment which he
found to be demeaning.

[
19
]

After several months, the husband decided he did not like the
apartment his father-in-law had selected for him.  He moved to a hotel which
was unsuitable for the children to visit.  He sent back the furniture the wife
had given him.  She told him she did not want it and would sell it.  He lasted
only a short while at several minimum wage jobs.

[
20
]

In September 2003, the husband and the children were in the
cafeteria at the Asper Campus when the husband caused an unpleasant scene.  He
was asked to put away food he had not purchased from the cafeteria and began
yelling and finally threw a plate onto the floor.  The children were crying.
The husband was banned from the Campus the next day which meant that he could
no longer attend the children’s daycare, school or participate in any of the
cultural and recreational offerings at the Campus.

[
21
]

After this incident, the wife decided to seek supervised access.
However, before she could do so, the husband withdrew his immigration
application and returned to Israel without any notice to her.  When the wife
found out he had returned to Israel, she withdrew her immigration sponsorship.

[
22
]

The husband remained in Israel for about nine months.  He would
call the children fairly regularly and the wife began noticing that the
children were becoming stressed and arguing with the husband, telling him that
mommy was not bad, grandpa did not kick him out, mommy is not fat and cruel,
etc.  The wife warned him that she would tape the calls and end them if he was
inappropriate.  She did tape the calls and would hang up if the children became
distraught.

[
23
]

The husband returned unexpectedly in June 2004.  He demanded to
see the children.  Because of his sudden departure and unannounced return, the
wife worried that he might abduct the children.  She decided that she would
attend the visits.  From June to September 2004, the visits were problematic.
At times, the wife had to have security guards or the police intervene when the
husband refused to let her and the children leave at the end of a visit in a
public place.

[
24
]

During this time, the husband picketed the Asper Campus on a
regular basis.  He wore a sandwich board protesting the fact that the Campus
would not allow him access to his children at their daycare.  The wife,
children and many of their friends saw the husband while he was picketing; the
wife found it embarrassing and the children were curious as to why their father
would be out with a sandwich board.  According to the wife, her friends began
to distance themselves and their children from her and the children to avoid
getting involved in the dispute.

[
25
]

The husband also chose to picket  the wife’s synagogue on the
High Holy Days, a local shopping mall and in front of his in-laws’ home.
Despite advice from his friends he refused to stop.

[
26
]

The parties appeared in court on September 20, 2004.  During the
hearing, the husband agreed not to picket any more.  A home assessment was
ordered and the husband was given twice weekly supervised access to the
children during the assessment process as well as daily telephone access.  It
was the expectation in court that the assessment would likely take two months
and the matter was made reviewable at that time.  Further, the court made a
prevention order under the
DVSA
legislation whereby the husband
was enjoined from contact with the wife and children, from attending the
children’s recreational activities and from his in-laws’ residence.

[
27
]

The husband was angry that daycare workers had filed affidavits
in support of the wife’s application for supervised access.  He began to
bombard the members of the daycare board with phone calls and e-mails.  He sent
e-mails to other prominent people connected to the Asper Campus.  The content
of the e-mails embarrassed the wife and raised concerns as to whether other
people’s children would be safe from the husband.

[
28
]

Despite the husband’s actions in the local community, by and
large, his visits with the children went fairly well.  However, he would not abide
by the agreed upon rules regarding pick-ups and drop-offs at his residence.  If
the husband raised inappropriate topics, the access supervisor was able to
redirect him.  However, he did not seem to learn from her redirection efforts.

[
29
]

In February 2005 both parties examined the access supervisor as a
third party witness.  After her testimony, the husband’s behaviour with the
children worsened.

[
30
]

As well, the husband’s behaviour in the community did not
improve.  Through counsel, the wife let the husband know she would be attending
the synagogue for several events in March so that he would not attend and be in
breach of the prevention order.  The husband attended the synagogue, ostensibly
to worship, and created an ugly scene in front of his children and others in
attendance at the event.  The wife called the police and the husband was
charged.

[
31
]

The access supervisor quit in April 2005 because the husband’s
behaviour during the visits deteriorated and he was no longer willing to
redirect his conversations with the children; consequently, the negative
remarks about their mother and family increased and the children became more
and more uncomfortable at the visits.  As well, the husband continued speaking
inappropriately to the children stating that mommy was trying to get rid of
him, mentioning future sleepovers at his place and the like.

[
32
]

The visits ceased although the phone calls continued.  Both
parties returned to court in June 2005.  By this time Dr. Linda Trigg, the
assessor, had completed her assessment.  The wife sought supervised access at
the Winnipeg Children’s Access Agency (“WCAA”); the husband wanted unsupervised
access and overnights.

[
33
]

At that court hearing, the court determined that the only
appropriate place that could supervise the husband’s access was the WCAA.
Knowing there was a waiting list, Jewish Child and Family Services Agency
(“JCFS”) was requested, but not ordered, to get involved in the interim.  The
court strengthened the earlier prevention order and forbade the husband from
attending synagogue when the wife or children would be present.  The court set
out a perimeter boundary around the Asper Campus within which the husband could
not enter.  The court also gave the wife permission to end the husband’s
telephone access if the husband spoke inappropriately with the children.

[
34
]

After some discussion, JCFS agreed to provide supervision for the
visits.  They made their expectations to the husband very clear in terms of the
conditions under which they would get involved.  While the husband did what was
asked, he continued to act out by testing all the conditions during visits.  At
no time was the husband able to acknowledge that but for their involvement, he
would not have been able to see the children at all.  By the end of their
involvement the husband was extremely hostile to the agency.

[
35
]

In December 2005, the husband’s access at the WCAA began.  Almost
immediately, he behaved inappropriately and visits were suspended.  After a
meeting they were reinstated and visits continued until April 2007.

[
36
]

The children’s demeanour improved once the visits were at the
WCAA.  They were relaxed about going and were much calmer coming home after a
visit.  The husband continued testing agency policies that he found demeaning
or insulting, but took direction from the visit monitor and accepted
confiscation of gifts or toys that were not allowed by agency policy.  His time
with the children was almost entirely child-centered and appropriate.

[
37
]

However, his activities in the community continued to cause
concern.  He was enraged about the children’s daycare workers and an employee
of JCFS providing affidavits on behalf of the wife in the domestic litigation.
He launched lawsuit after lawsuit.  He gave interviews in the community
newspaper about his family situation and what he believed to be the wife’s
parents’ influence in the community.  He contacted parents of the children’s
classmates.  He sent information from a daycare worker’s personal domestic file
to parents of the daycare.  The last straw came when he sent probate
information about the wife’s grandfather’s estate to a host of community
members.

[
38
]

In February 2006, the wife returned to court and the court
ordered that the husband be forbidden access to any court files other than his
own, and that he could access that file only under the supervision of court
staff.  He was also forbidden to contact staff and parents of the daycare,
school and the Asper Campus.  He appealed this order and the Court of Appeal
varied it slightly to permit access to files in the course of any employment as
a law student.

[
39
]

The husband continued his vendetta against the daycare and one
board member in particular.  In January 2005, the board member went to the
police and the husband was charged with uttering threats.  As part of his bail
conditions he was ordered to have no contact with the complainant.  The charges
were stayed in March 2005 in return for the husband entering a peace bond.  As
well, the daycare board obtained an injunction against the husband forbidding
him from attending near the board member or from violating her privacy.

[
40
]

However, the board member continued getting harassing telephone
calls.  After an investigation, the police arrested the husband and charged him
with criminal harassment and violation of the peace bond.  Ultimately, in 2006,
the husband pled guilty to violation of the peace bond and the harassment
charge was dropped.

[
41
]

During this time, the supervised visits with the children
continued, and based on the monitors’ reports, were for the most part a
success.  The second assessment was completed in December 2006.  It
recommended, amongst other things, that supervised access at the WCAA continue
for the next year.

[
42
]

In October 2006 the board of directors of the wife’s synagogue
banned the husband from attending its premises.

[
43
]

In the latter part of 2006, the husband resolved all his other
outstanding lawsuits.  He further agreed that he would not commence any other
litigation against those he had sued until his children were adults.  In
essence, the husband basically agreed he was a vexatious litigant.

[
44
]

The trial commenced in February 2007 and finished in the later
part of May, having continued for 37 days during this time.

HUSBAND’S CREDIBILITY/DEMEANOUR

[
45
]

Before examining the legal issues, I must comment on the
husband’s behaviour in court, towards his family, the community and when
dealing with any persons in authority, and the impact that behaviour has had on
his credibility.

[
46
]

I found the husband to be the most disrespectful person who has
ever appeared before me.  Even allowing for the stress of representing himself
in a lengthy trial with a myriad of legal and emotional issues, I found his
manner excessive and almost uncontrollable.  He continually disregarded my
instructions/admonishments, showed no regard for courtroom decorum, and
interrupted and erupted whenever he felt like it.  His self control was
minimal.

[
47
]

In order to manage his behaviour I was required to use measures
such as the use of hand signals to signal that he must stop talking, the
imposition of “time outs”, sending him out into the hallway so counsel could
read documents uninterrupted, and instructing witnesses not to answer his
questions until he was seated so that the witness would not be bombarded with
further questions and argument in the middle of an answer.  If an evidentiary
ruling went against him, he usually reacted by threatening to call a prominent
member of the Jewish community as a witness.

[
48
]

Although a qualified lawyer in Israel, the husband’s fixation on
a “conflict of interest” between what he called the wife’s family’s power and
influence in the Jewish community and their perceived influence on the Jewish
institutions from which he has now been banned caused him to lead a myriad of
irrelevant evidence, most of which harmed his case.

[
49
]

For example (but one of many), the husband called both the rabbi
and the president of the synagogue which had banned the husband from its
premises.  On this point, the evidence had been that there was a prevention
order preventing the husband from attending the synagogue when the wife was to
be there, and that there had been some harassing behavior towards the wife in
the presence of others at the synagogue before the general ban was put into
place.

[
50
]

Once these two witnesses had given their testimony, I had learned
of the husband’s disrespectful behavior towards the rabbi and others both
inside and outside the place of worship, and even during the ceremony of
worship itself.  As a result, I conclude that the husband’s inability to
control himself in court is not simply attributable to the stress of the trial
itself but extends into any place where he feels the wife’s family’s influence
stretched, including the synagogue, regardless of the sacred nature of that
place of worship.

[
51
]

In Israel, the husband held the relatively senior rank of captain
in the Israeli army.  When he returned to Israel in 2003, he was called up for
reserve duty, so I assume that he was able to follow orders and behave
appropriately in a military environment.  Knowing this background, his
inability to take direction, whether from the court, the visit supervisors or
from his friends, was all the more unfathomable.  When queried on this point,
the husband’s evidence was that he could and did follow orders when “his life
was on the line” but fighting for his children was far more important than life
itself.  I find this distinction means the husband sees himself free to act out
whenever he wishes if he feels it appropriate to do so.  I therefore question
what parts of his behaviour are calculated and what parts he simply cannot
control.  Certainly, when told by a court that his behaviour was “torpedoing”
his case, the expectation is that the behaviour will improve: for the husband,
it did – for about 30 minutes.

[
52
]

Many times during the trial, I was reminded of a two year old
having a tantrum saying, “I’ll stop if you give me what I want.”  Indeed, in
evidence, the husband said, “the only solution to my problem is for me to see
my kids.”  He blames his anger and outbursts on all the external forces
preventing him from getting his wish.  The list is long and includes the wife’s
family and their perceived influence in the Jewish community, the wife’s
lawyer, the daycare, most Jewish organizations, the court backlog, the access
supervisors’ restrictions on his role as a father and the failure of many
persons in authority to sit down and talk with him.  However, in my view, the
husband’s version of talking would be for him to harangue and overwhelm the
other side until he got what he wanted.

[
53
]

In examining the husband’s attitude and demeanour throughout the
trial, it became clear he would say whatever he thought most expedient in the
heat of the moment.  He pleaded guilty to a charge of making a harassing phone
call, but tried for some “wiggle room” by saying that his lawyer and not
himself, entered the plea.  He pointed to the settlement of all his various
lawsuits and the agreement that he was in essence a vexatious litigant, as
proof that all that was behind him, yet it was very clear in his handling of
witnesses who had been part of any of those lawsuits that his anger at the
various people and institutions who he felt had wronged him was still clearly
present.  His witness list included many of the people connected to his other
litigation, even though most of these witnesses had only slight or tangential
relevance to the issues before the court.

[
54
]

At times, the husband out and out lied to the court.  While the
husband was on the witness stand giving his evidence, he was first suspended
and then terminated from the access agency.  He was asked what he had told the
children in their nightly phone call.  Despite knowing that the wife tapes all
calls, he denied telling the children he was on a “time out,” denied that he
had talked to them about the nice judge who had three children herself, denied
that he had said he and mommy were seeing the nice judge every day, and denied
saying that soon he would see the children more and without other people
around.

[
55
]

The tape was played and indeed the husband had said all those
things and more.  His explanation was that it had been a terrible day for him
as it was the day he found out that, despite his reinstatement at the access
agency three days before, they were now terminating his use of the centre based
on his flouting of their authority the night before.

[
56
]

I note that the husband, when confronted with promises he had
made and then broken (for example telling the motions judge that he would stop
picketing or signing an agreement with the access agency that he would not
communicate except in writing), had elaborate rationales for why he was
justified in breaking his word.  Regarding the promise to the judge, he said he
thought he was agreeing to this because she said he could see his kids in a few
months and when he could not, he felt the judge had broken her word first.  He
said he only signed the agreement so he could see the children, and anyway, a
phone call to the agency he made was only regarding a fax he had sent and so
did not count as a communication.

[
57
]

Finally, in argument, the husband said he was going to apologize
for his courtroom behaviour.  He gave a litany of excuses and rationales for
his actions. He then moved to a different topic, saying; “well the apology is
done.”  However, I had heard no apology and when I commented on that fact, he
seemed quite startled and finally offered his apology to the court.

[
58
]

As a result of the many overstatements, misstatements and
fabrications of the husband, I find that I am unable to rely on his evidence.
Where it conflicts with that of any other witness, I prefer the other evidence
than that of the husband.

CUSTODY – JOINT OR SOLE?

[
59
]

The husband urges the court to impose joint custody.  He accepts,
albeit reluctantly, that the wife is the primary caregiver.

[
60
]

The wife is adamantly opposed to joint custody.  She points to
the husband’s behaviour and character and says it would be impossible to have
any meaningful dialogue about the children, let alone share decision-making.

[
61
]

I accept the wife’s position.  In my view, it would be a disaster
for the children and their mother if the husband was allowed to have input into
their upbringing.  He demonstrated, time and time again throughout the trial,
that he is incapable of letting go of issues and what he perceives as slights.
He showed some small ability to appreciate another point of view, but that
positive factor was offset by his unjustified view that the wife’s family and
their influence is the cause of all his problems rather than his own actions.

[
62
]

There is no doubt that the husband loves the children.  However,
a joint custodial arrangement requires respect and co-operation between the
parents and I see no evidence that the husband is capable of putting aside his
own issues to work with the wife in the interests of the children.

[
63
]

Accordingly, the wife will have sole custody of the children.

ACCESS:  TERMINATED, SUPERVISED OR UNSUPERVISED?

[
64
]

Clearly, the husband is a difficult person.  He has alienated
many of his friends, most professionals and most members of the Jewish
community with whom he has come into contact.  However, the issue is not
whether the court, or anyone else, likes the man, but whether, given whom he
is, he can contribute to the happiness and emotional well-being of his
children.

[
65
]

Complicating matters is the fact that during the course of the
trial, the husband’s visits with the children were first suspended (for
speaking to other parents after the children had left about his intention to
“crucify” the executive director of the WCAA on the witness stand the next day)
and then terminated for breaking one of the conditions of his reinstatement
some three days later.  As a result of these incidents, the wife amended her
position at trial to request that access be terminated.

[
66
]

The husband requests “regular access” to include alternating
weekends and some weekday time.

[
67
]

As access issues have been problematic since the beginning, I
will review the history in some detail.

[
68
]

Once the court determined that, pending an assessment, visits
were to be supervised, the parties hired a supervisor selected by the husband.
She provided supervision for twice weekly visits, for some six months.  She
ultimately quit when the husband’s behaviour and demeanour toward the children
deteriorated.  He would no longer accept her corrections to move off topics
such as the children’s mother and family.  She found his behaviour intolerable.

[
69
]

Dr. Trigg’s first assessment was conducted early in 2005 while
the supervised visits were in place.  She noted the husband’s difficult
personality, his inability to control himself and his self pre-occupation.  She
commented on his need to control the agenda, his inability to take personal
responsibility for his actions and his constant need to discuss his legal
problems in front of the children.

[
70
]

Dr. Trigg concluded that the children were attached to their
father and would mourn their loss if he was no longer in their life.  However,
she found the problematic behaviour of the husband was such that he should only
see them under the supervision of the WCAA, a place where the rules were clear
and not open to interpretation.

[
71
]

In June 2005, the parties returned to court after the assessment
was complete.  The issues before the court included the husband’s behaviour
during the nightly telephone calls, his picketing of the Asper Campus, his
conduct at the synagogue, and his access to the children.

[
72
]

The court ordered that there be supervised access at the WCAA
and, as there was a six month waiting list, requested that JCFS consider
supervising visits in the meantime.  As well, under the
DVSA

legislation, the court strengthened the terms of the prevention order relating
to the Asper Campus, the synagogue and the husband’s telephone calls with the
children.

[
73
]

After discussion with the husband, JCFS agreed to supervise some
visits.  They required the husband to take certain courses, which he did.  They
set out rules for the visits and found themselves immersed in a continuing
power struggle with the husband over what to bring for the visits, how to
behave and what to say and not say at the visits.  The husband would call the
agency repeatedly and basically presented as threatening, demanding and
inappropriate.  He challenged every instruction given to him, often at the
expense of time with his children.  In the words of the supervisor, the
husband’s actions continually undermined the support he wanted from the
agency.  In reviewing the evidence of the husband’s behaviour during this time
frame, I am again struck by his lack of appreciation that the agency was going
beyond its mandate in providing supervision to him.

[
74
]

In December 2005, the family was accepted at the WCAA.  After
three visits, this agency suspended the husband for “numerous and repeated
breaches to the Service Agreement … and a demonstrated disregard for the
authority of staff.”  After a meeting with the husband, the executive director
set out ten expectations of the husband and visits resumed.

[
75
]

In analyzing the problems, it is clear that they were more of the
same – not having the children ready to leave on time, repeatedly calling the
agency, disobeying the rules and ignoring staff instructions.

[
76
]

However, after that meeting, visits resumed and continued until
April 2007.  During the sixteen months of supervised visits, most of them
went very well.  It is clear that the husband chafed under the agency’s authority
and continually tested their boundaries, but his actual interactions with the
children were, by and large, perfectly appropriate.

[
77
]

Dr. Trigg conducted a second assessment in the fall of 2006.  At
that time she felt the husband had made some progress.  She felt he had gained
a modicum of insight into what had gone wrong.  She said his parenting skills
had gone from “abominable and harmful to his children” to “superb.”  However,
his battles and interactions with the Jewish community continued to be unhealthy
and counter-productive to building a healthy life in Canada.  She was uncertain
whether the fact the children were more relaxed and comfortable with their
father was a product of the husband’s changed behaviour or whether it was the
tightly controlled protection of the access agency which allowed the children
to enjoy their time with their father without worrying he would stray into the
negativity so prevalent with the earlier access supervisors.

[
78
]

As a result of Dr. Trigg’s inability to determine what was
allowing the children to feel so much more comfortable with their father, she
recommended that supervised access continue for another year.  She set out a
number of recommendations which the husband was to follow during that year.
These recommendations included refraining from picketing, apologizing to the
wife and her family, refraining from any public action or publicity, refocusing
his life and studying or working full time, ceasing to blame others for his
problems, consulting an expert about acceptable Canadian behaviour and
accepting the past and moving forward in productive ways.  She further
suggested that another assessment be conducted at the end of the year to assess
whether the husband has made the required changes and determine whether unsupervised
access would be appropriate.

[
79
]

I do not find Dr. Trigg’s recommendations particularly helpful.
In my view, many of those recommendations would require the husband to become a
different person, when the issue before the court is what should happen now, in
light of the children’s clear wish to see their father and in light of how the
husband chooses to live his life.

[
80
]

These children unfortunately have a father who has behaved in
ways far off the mainstream of life in Winnipeg.  He has done foolish things,
embarrassing things and harmful things.  He has harassed people.  He has almost
no ability to self monitor or ask himself whether his children would be proud
of his behaviour or humiliated by it.  In large part, I expect that if the
children were old enough, they would be humiliated if they knew of many of the
things he has done.

[
81
]

On the other hand, the assessor found a marked improvement in the
husband’s behavior at the time of the second assessment.  She likened his
courtroom antics while she was giving her evidence to his behaviour during the
first assessment, but said that he had shown some improvement during the second
one.  As well, she noted the parent-child interactions showed marked
improvement.  During the home visits, she found his parenting to be superb and
exemplary.

[
82
]

The husband asks me to consider that he comes from a different
culture where, he says, people are less deferential to authority, louder and
more expressive than Canadians.  He points to the fact that the children are
half-Israeli and need to know that part of their heritage.  He says he is
devoted to his children and wants them to be proud of him.

[
83
]

I have reviewed the access supervisors’ notes from each and every
weekly visit over the sixteen months of visits.  The notes are detailed and
chronicle the entirety of each two hour visit.  I agree with Dr. Trigg that the
husband comes across as an exemplary parent: he is sensitive to the children’s
wishes, playful, imaginative and provides good parenting in a very artificial
environment.

[
84
]

The husband blames his “misbehaviour” on the “absurd” nature of
the WCAA’s rules and procedures.  He finds it humiliating to have to follow
their rules and as a result engages in a stealth war, trying to wiggle around
every rule he can.  For example, he knows that the policy is no photos of
anyone but the children and him.  Rather than accept this as the price he has
to pay for seeing his children, he continually brings pictures, from the
internet or otherwise which have other people in them to test the rules.  He
also brought Ninja Turtles, toys banned as each turtle carries a sword or stick
which could be interpreted as a weapon, despite being told not to.  When
suspended, he chose to consider the meeting to decide whether to reinstate
service as an opportunity to offer “constructive criticism” to the board member
present, rather than apologize for his rule breaches that brought about the
suspension.

[
85
]

There is no doubt that supervised access is an artificial
construct which can cause both parent and child to chafe from time to time.  I
agree many of the policies may seem heavy-handed, but the WCAA is trying to
offer a safe environment without knowing the background or “hot button issues”
of each family to whom they offer service.  As a result, they have developed
policies which, while providing a neutral space, do inhibit typical
parent-child interactions.  However, the intention is that use of the centre is
to be a short term measure, used to prove whether the visiting parent is
capable of unsupervised contact or is unable to offer the children anything
positive, whereby contact is ended.  What is clear is that the centre is a
place of last resort for children to see a parent.

[
86
]

In his battles with the WCAA, the husband has chosen to put his
interests over the children and for the moment has lost that place of last
resort for the children to see their father.  In my view, he can blame no one
but himself for continuing his pattern of sabotaging his relationship with his
children.

[
87
]

The wife says this pattern of self destructive behaviour warrants
a termination of access.  She points to the husband’s continual denigration of
herself and her family, his questionable behaviour in the Jewish community and
his inability to resolve his anger and says that although the children are well
adjusted now, they may not be so in the future.

[
88
]

There is no doubt that to deny access is a remedy of last
resort.  See
Jennings v. Garrett
(2004),
2004 CanLII 17126 (ON SC)
, 5 R.F.L. (6
th
)
319 (Ont.Sup.C.J.), at paras.
128 and 129
:

¶128   There is a presumption that regular access
by a non-custodial parent is in the best interests of children.  The right of a
child to visit with a non-custodial parent, to know and maintain or form an
attachment to a non-custodial parent is a fundamental right and should only be
forfeited in the most extreme and unusual circumstances.  To deny access to a
parent is a remedy of last resort.  See
Jafari v. Dadar
,
[1996] N.B.J.
No. 387 (N.B.Q.B.)
.

¶129   A review of the case law reveals that
there are no standard criteria for termination of access within the best
interests test.  Madam Justice Abella noted at para. 34 of M. (B.P.) v. M.
(B.L.D.E.) (1992),
1992 CanLII 8642 (ON CA)
, 42 R.F.L. (3d) 349 (Ont.C.A.):

It is not a question of what standard
should be used to deprive a parent of access, it is a question of what standard
should be used in deciding what form of access, if any, should be ordered. The
answer is clear from the statute:  the standard is the child's best interests.

[
89
]

The wife relies on a number of cases:
N.J.F. v. D.K.A.

(1995),
1995 CanLII 16361 (MB QB)
, 101 Man.R. (2d) 70 (M.B.Q.B.);
Dixon v. Hinsley
(2001),

2001 CanLII 38986 (ON CJ)
, 22 R.F.L. (5th) 55 (Ont. C.J.);
Jennings. v. Garrett
,
supra
,

M. (B.P.) v. M. (B.L.D.E.)
(1992),
1992 CanLII 8642 (ON CA)
, 42 R.F.L. (3d) 349 (Ont.C.A.);
and
Stewart v. Bachan
,
[2003] O.J. No. 433 (QL) (Ont. C.J.)
.

[
90
]

However, most of these cases differ from this one in one crucial
element: here, the children do benefit from their relationship with their
father.  Even when his parenting was “abominable,” the assessor found that they
would experience feelings of loss and grief, not relief, if their father was to
disappear from their lives.  Now, when he has improved his parenting skills to
the “exemplary” level, albeit under close supervision, I would expect that the
loss and grief would be even worse for them.

[
91
]

I therefore reject the wife’s request to terminate access.

[
92
]

The issue is thus, what level of access is appropriate.  While
the husband argues that his behaviour would improve if only he had regular
access, I find this to be a parent-centred argument rather than a child-centred
one.

[
93
]

While the husband provided excellent parenting to the children at
the WCAA, I have grave concerns about his ability to control himself when he is
not able to get what he wants, when he wants.  Both inside and outside court,
his reaction to being thwarted is to erupt into threats and agitated argument
with no regard for those around him.  Were he allowed to see the children in an
unsupervised environment and was treated, in his view, disrespectfully by
anyone I fear that he would “lose it” and the children could be put at risk.

[
94
]

As the husband has already put his relationship with the children
at risk by putting his need to argue with the WCAA ahead of accepting their
rules as the price he has to pay to see the children he has demonstrated his
inability to prioritize.  This, coupled with a demonstrated lack of self
control, convinces me that the husband is not ready for unsupervised access.
While I do not accept that the husband must transform himself as suggested by
the assessor, he must demonstrate at least that he can control himself
sufficiently for the court to be sure he can put aside his own issues and
battles to protect his young children.

[
95
]

While supervised access is normally viewed as a short term
solution, I agree with Blishen, J. in
Jennings v. Garrett
,
supra
,
at para.
139
, where she says:

¶139   There may be occasions, however, where
medium or longer term supervised access is in the child's best interests.
Professor Martha Bailey of the Faculty of Law at Queen's University questions
what she considers to be the doctrinaire approach which assumes that long term
supervised access is not in the best interests of the child and notes that this
approach may undermine the child's right to maintain personal contact with the
parent except where contrary to the child's best interests.  In her article,
"Supervised Access: A Long Term Solution?" 37 Family and Conciliation
Courts Rev. 478 (October 1999), she states the following at p. 480:

The issue of whether long term
supervised access is in the best interests of the child must be determined on a
case by case basis, taking into consideration all circumstances relevant to the
best interests of the child. The question then is whether there are any
circumstances under which long term supervised access will be in the best
interests of the child, even where unsupervised access is not a future option.

[
96
]

In considering the best interests of these children, I note that
the children are deeply attached to their father.  Indeed, the older child
clearly states that she wants to see more of her father.  He does add value to
their lives in that he is inventive and playful in his interactions with them.
Further, despite the husband’s inappropriate behaviour, they are well adjusted,
happy and relaxed.  Accordingly, despite the artificial construct of supervised
access, I find that it is appropriate for these children.

[
97
]

While I cannot predict when, if ever, the husband might be able
to bring his emotions under control so as to have more normalized access, I
think the first step would be for him to make his peace with the past.  He may
well have been treated badly at times, but his reactions to that treatment have
been extreme and harmful to himself and his relationship with the children.
Despite his flaws, the husband has many good qualities as a parent and he needs
to accent those positives and move forward.

[
98
]

In this case, there are two reasons to continue to require the
visits to be supervised.  The first is that someone needs to be present to step
in and remove the children in case the husband loses control of himself and
puts the children at risk.  The second is that someone needs to ensure that the
husband does not cause the children emotional harm by talking to them about the
court process or speaking poorly of their mother, her family and the “powerful”
people in the Jewish community.

[
99
]

In my view, what the children need on these visits is a person
who will intervene only if their father crosses the line in these areas.  The
balance of the rules of the WCAA, such as no discussing schools and extracurricular
activities, no making of future promises, no photos of extended family,
friends, pets or movie stars and the like, are not necessary for this parent
and these children.

[
100
]

Who then could
perform this role?  The wife makes no suggestions as she wanted the access
terminated.  The assessor recommended the WCAA but they refuse to offer
continued services and in any event, I find that the husband’s behaviour with
the children during the actual visits is sufficiently appropriate that their
very strict rules about the content of parent-child interactions are no longer
required.

[
101
]

The husband
suggests that a friend of his, Susan Koskinen, be appointed supervisor.  I note
that the assessor rejected her as a possibility because she did not have all
the facts about the husband’s misdeeds and misbehaviour.

[
102
]

However, when
Ms Koskinen testified, I was very impressed with her stability and outlook on
life.  Many of the husband’s misbehaviours were put to her on cross-examination
and I find that she reacted appropriately to them.  Further, her calm and
thoughtful demeanour would be an asset to the children.  She said that should
she be able to participate with the children, she would be honoured.  She saw
herself in the role of “aunt” and would do whatever she could to ease tensions.

[
103
]

In order to be
involved, however, she would also have to act as the children’s protector in
the event the husband “lost it” during a visit.  In assessing her evidence, I
find she is capable of fulfilling the role of friend to the children and putting
that role ahead of her friendship to the husband.

[
104
]

Nevertheless,
because of that friendship, I find it necessary to set out the “terms of her
engagement” as a supervisor.

[
105
]

If Ms Koskinen
agrees to act as supervisor I would expect her to sign an undertaking to the
court that she would participate in the visits as the children’s friend.  The
undertaking would simply set out a promise that if the husband loses control of
himself, she will remove the children from the situation and return them to
their mother immediately.  If the husband talked to them about court or spoke
disrespectfully about the children’s family or friends and refused to stop,
again, she would undertake to remove the children and return them to their
mother.

[
106
]

In my view,
this arrangement is the “last resort” for these children.  If the husband
cannot comply with these minimal conditions of good behaviour, then the other
positive things he has to offer the children have no long term value to them.
Accordingly, in the event that the children have to be returned to their mother
early on more than two occasions, Ms Koskinen’s supervision will be terminated
and visits will cease.

[
107
]

Further, if Ms
Koskinen refuses or is unable to accept this role, I find that there is no
acceptable access alternative before me which will protect the children unless
the husband is able to persuade the WCAA to reinstate service.  If she is not
prepared to get involved, I conclude that, on a risk/reward analysis, it is
better for the children to have no contact with their father, unless through
the WCAA, than be placed in potentially dangerous circumstances with him
alone.

[
108
]

Assuming Ms
Koskinen gives the required undertaking, the husband’s access will take place
twice weekly.  Ms Koskinen will be present at all times. There will be a
weekday visit for two hours and a weekend visit for four hours.  I have no
evidence about the children’s activities or Ms Koskinen’s schedule and so do
not set the exact days and times of the visits.  If the husband and wife are
unable to agree on the time and days of the visits, I will set them.

[
109
]

If Ms Koskinen
is unable to give the undertaking and the WCAA is prepared to be involved, the
husband’s access will be once weekly on the day and times that the WCAA can
offer service.  If this occurs, I find there is no need for continuous
monitoring of each visit and intermittent supervision will be satisfactory.
The husband will be expected to comply with all the WCAA rules and conditions.

[
110
]

Further, the
wife may take the children on holidays for up to three weeks per year.  She
will give the husband two weeks written notice of her choice of dates, during
which times his visits will be cancelled.  The husband will have one four hour
make-up visit per week of holidays, which visit will be made up within two
weeks of the wife’s holiday departure or return.

[
111
]

If the wife
wishes to holiday outside Canada, she may do so and the husband’s consent to
travel is dispensed with.  However, she must give the husband notice, in
writing, of the travel plans including destination and contact numbers, two
weeks in advance of her departure.

[
112
]

In finding that
supervised access with Ms Koskinen is in the children’s best interests I have
set out minimal boundaries for the husband.  I am aware that he has a
significant problem following rules.  I do not think the conditions I have
imposed are “rules,” but simply things that need to be in place in order that
the children can continue having a healthy relationship with their father.  I
expect his parenting during visits to continue to be “superb” and “exemplary”
because that is what the children need from him.

TELEPHONE ACCESS

[
113
]

Presently the
husband is allowed a 15 minute call per evening with the children.  The wife
tapes the calls and has the authority to end them if the husband strays into
unhealthy topics, such as name calling and denigration of the wife or her
family.  Some of the calls have been ended early; in those he has been truly
insensitive to the children and their needs.

[
114
]

The wife seeks
some flexibility around the calls because they sometimes interfere with the
children’s activities.

[
115
]

In my view, now
that the husband will be seeing the children twice weekly, daily calls are
unnecessary.  I will allow two calls per week, again for 15 minutes, with the
time and days to be set by agreement or by me.  As I ordered during the trial,
the television will be turned off during the calls.  However, if the access is
at the WCAA, the calls will continue as in the interim order. The wife will
continue to tape the calls and will have the ability to end them if she finds
them distressing for the children.

[
116
]

When the wife
is on holidays with the children, the calls will continue.

NON-REMOVAL

[
117
]

Both husband
and wife seek a non-removal order, preventing the other from taking or moving
the children outside the province.  There is nothing in the evidence which
would lead me to grant one against the wife.  She is securely attached to
Winnipeg and has no plans to move.  However, in the event she does wish to move
in the future, she must give the husband 60 days written notice of her plans.

[
118
]

I am prepared
to order that the husband not remove the children from Manitoba.  While I do
not think he would do so, his impulsive nature and “hair-splitting” attitude
around rules convince me that it is appropriate to spell out the fact that he
may not remove the children from Manitoba without the permission of the wife or
the court.  The order will also contain a peace officer assistance clause.

husband’S PASSPORT

[
119
]

The assessor
recommended that the husband’s passport be surrendered during visits.  The
husband found this, as he put it, “demeaning,” but agreed to do so and
suggested the wife’s lawyer keep it.  In my view, the surrender of the passport
on a twice weekly basis is unworkable and would impose too great a burden on
any third party.  Although he is impulsive, I do not find the husband to be a
flight risk.  He accepts that the children’s lives are here and is aware that

,

PREVENTION ORDER

[
120
]

In September
2004, the court granted, on an interim basis, a prevention order under the
DVSA
.
The order basically prevented the husband from following, contacting or
communicating with the wife and children.  He was not allowed to attend or
enter anywhere they resided or regularly attended, including the daycare,
school, grandparents’ home and the places of the children’s extra curricular
activities while those activities were on.  The husband was also ordered to see
a psychiatrist.

[
121
]

As the
husband’s behaviour became more and more outrageous, the wife returned to court
for more protection.  In June 2005, as a result of the husband’s picketing and
behaviour at the synagogue, the court set out a perimeter boundary around the
Asper Campus where the children attended daycare and school and ordered that
the husband not attend the synagogue if the wife notified him that she and the
children were going to be there.

[
122
]

However, these
restraints only appeared to whet the husband’s imagination in terms of what to
do next in his battles with the wife’s family and the Jewish community.  During
the period of time that JCFS was supervising his visits, he began trolling
through court files to see what information he could find and use against those
who he perceived to be his enemies.  As mentioned earlier, he circulated
portions of an affidavit filed by a daycare worker in her domestic litigation.
He sent cryptic emails to all and sundry.  Finally, the last straw came when he
began circulating probate documents containing financial information relative
to the wife’s grandparents’ estates to prominent members of the Jewish
community, parents of children attending his daughters’ daycare and school and
members of the Asper Campus.

[
123
]

In February
2006, the court found that the husband’s use of these documents was
psychological and emotional abuse of the wife and the children, constituting
domestic violence.  In essence the husband was prohibited from inspecting,
copying or disseminating any court document without leave of the court except
for files where he was a party.  Further the court staff was ordered to
supervise and monitor him when he wanted to inspect the domestic file or any
file to which he was a party.  The husband was also prohibited from sending
documents and from communicating with parents and staff of the daycare and the
Asper Campus about the estate or the domestic file.  He was ordered not to
breach the privacy of the children, the wife, and her family.  Finally, he was
not allowed to receive reports of any type relating to the children.

[
124
]

The Court of
Appeal varied this order slightly, by permitting unsupervised access to court files
if, as a law student, the husband’s employer required him to do so in the
course of his employment and by delineating that the non contact or non
communication ban was with persons whom he knew to be parents or staff of the
daycare, school or Asper Campus.  He further was allowed access to written
reports regarding the children’s medical and dental issues.

[
125
]

Since the last
order, there has been relative peace for the children, the wife and her family,
although I note that the husband appears to search the online Court Registry
and Companies Branch documents regularly in his quest for information about
people with whom he has an issue.  In argument, he defended his prying into
people’s lives as justified, claiming that “knowledge is power.”

[
126
]

The wife seeks
to continue the order with small variations and the husband asks the court to
rescind it in its entirety.  He is particularly concerned with the prohibition
from attending near the Asper Campus.

[
127
]

Before any
prevention order was in place, the husband was issued a notice under
The

Petty Trespasses Act
, R.S.M. 1987, c. P50, that he was not welcome on
the premises of the Asper Campus.  This notice was issued after the September
2003 incident in the cafeteria and in effect, bans the husband from the
facility.  This meant he could not visit the children at the daycare centre or
school or participate in any of the sporting, cultural and social activities of
the Campus, the hub of Jewish life in Winnipeg.

[
128
]

While the
husband has made overtures to the board of directors of the Campus, their
position is that there is no point in reconsidering the ban as long as there
are other court orders which prevent the husband’s attendance.

[
129
]

I find, at the
present time the order, as it relates to the Asper Campus, is too wide in its
scope.  I understand fully how, in light of the husband’s escalating negative
behaviour, it seemed prudent simply to prohibit him at all times from this
locale, but an order of this nature should be crafted as narrowly as possible
to prohibit contact between the parties, rather than prohibit contact with a
place.  I note, for example, that while the husband is prohibited from
attending another local swimming pool and skating arena, the order only
prevents his attendance at those places during the times of the children’s
lessons.  Further, the prohibition as it relates to the synagogue (prior to its
own ban) only required that the husband not attend if he knew the wife was
going to be there or to leave if he discovered her present on the premises.

[
130
]

It is true that
the wife spends some time and the children a great deal of time at the Campus,
but I do not think they should have, in essence, exclusive occupation of this
place on the off-chance they wish to attend outside of the school and day care
hours.

[
131
]

In this
situation, particularly given the unique cultural services the Campus offers, I
am only prepared to continue to order that the husband not attend the Asper
Campus lands and premises weekdays between 8:30 am and 6:00 pm. when school,
daycare or summer camps are in session.  However, if the wife provides written
notice to the husband that either she or the children will be attending an out
of school hours event, whether related to the children or the wife, the husband
is prohibited from attending during the hours any or all of them will be
there.

[
132
]

The prevention
order was expanded to include the entire Asper Campus as a result of the
husband’s picketing and hanging around the outskirts of the Campus.  Clearly,
these activities have become a counter-productive activity for the husband and,
should he decide to resume them, he does so at his peril.  He still needs to
address the issue of the general ban from the Asper Campus lands and premises
and, whatever the difference between Israeli and Canadian protest modes, the
husband is very aware that this type of activity will only be a negative
influence on his wish for reinstatement to this Canadian institution.

[
133
]

I note that the
wife interpreted the last order that she had to give the husband written notice
of any synagogue attendance through her lawyer and I want to make it clear
that, should the general ban imposed by the Campus and/or synagogue be lifted,
she may write the husband directly, by ordinary mail, to give notice of
attendance at the Asper Campus or synagogue.  The husband will be deemed to
have received her notice two days after the date of the notice.  In the event
that the husband and the wife and/or the children are present by accident, the
husband is required to vacate the premises immediately.

[
134
]

As far as the
other various provisions of the prevention order are concerned, I determine
that most of them should remain in place, subject to some small variations.  In
my view, the provisions of the other orders have granted the wife and children
some peace and that should continue.  Further, the husband needs to concentrate
on his relationship with his children and as his unacceptable behaviour toward
them has improved while he was under these court restrictions, it will be to
their benefit that he continues to be governed by them.  However, I note that
the prohibition on access to court records provides an exception should the
husband be employed as a law student.  In light of what I understand to be the
husband’s status should he pass the National Accreditation Committee exams, he
may become qualified to practice law in his own right.  If, indeed, this comes
to pass, he may have access to court files on the same terms as set out by the
Court of Appeal.

[
135
]

I accept the
wife’s request that the court add a distance boundary around her home and order
that the husband may not attend within 100 metres of her residence.

[
136
]

In argument,
the wife agreed that the husband could receive copies of the children’s school
reports and I so order.  As well, if the school wishes to resume parent-teacher
interviews with the father off the premises of the Campus or on the Campus if
the ban is lifted and after 6:00 pm, they may do so.  He will continue to be

[
137
]

The wife asks
the court to rule that the husband cannot come back to court in future without
some sort of pre-screening by a judge.  She says he has made her life miserable
by filing motion after motion in the lead up to the trial.  She points to his
myriad of other civil litigation and says that if the court does not restrict
his ability to seek relief from the court now, she will be forever entangled in
ongoing litigation.

[
138
]

She relies on

S. 73(1)
of
The
Court of Queen’s Bench Act
, S.M. 1988-89, c. 4 –
Cap. C280, which states:

73(1)   Where a judge
is satisfied, on application, that a person, persistently and without
reasonable grounds, is

proceedings in the court; or

(c) the person shall not
institute a further proceeding; or

(d) a proceeding instituted by
the person not be continued,

except with leave of a judge.

[
139
]

In my view, it
is not appropriate at this time to limit the husband’s access to the court.
While I sympathize with the wife’s wish to bring her domestic litigation to an
end, the reality is that in high conflict families where one or both parents
can not modify their behaviour for the children’s sake, the court provides the
only dispute resolution mechanism possible.  Further, the court’s role is to
determine the best interests of the children and these interests may evolve
over time, even though the parents’ positions do not evolve.

[
140
]

Given the
access regime I have imposed, it may well be that in future, if it is
successful, the best interests of the children may require a different type of
access arrangement than that imposed by me now.

[
141
]

However, it
seems to me that the children would benefit if there was a “ceasefire” imposed
for a period of time, in order to assess the success of the access arrangements
I have ordered.  Given the husband’s past behaviour, I doubt any judge would be
prepared to consider a variation request by him until a lengthy period of
uneventful supervised access had taken place.  Accordingly, I direct that the
husband may not make any court application regarding his access for one year,
without prior leave of the court, unless there has been non-compliance on the
part of the wife with my access order.

[
142
]

As far as the
provisions of the prevention order I have granted are concerned, it may be that
if the husband does normalize his behaviour in the community in the future,
that some of the provisions relating to the children and attendance at their
activities could be loosened.  Again I would expect that the husband would have
to point to a lengthy period of uninterrupted good behaviour before a court
would consider this.  Accordingly, I direct that the husband may not make any
application regarding the prevention order, without prior leave of the court,
for one year.

]

The wife relies
on an agreement signed by the parties in advance of their marriage.  This
agreement provided that each would keep his or her own property as separate and
only assets registered in the joint names of the parties would be shared on
separation.

agreement is defined in
Section 1(1)
of
The

,
C.C.S.M. c. F25 ( the “

or marital agreement, or

(b) any separation
agreement, or

(c) release or quit claim
deed,

in writing, or any other written
agreement or other writing between spouses, made within Manitoba or elsewhere
before or after the coming into force of this Act and either during marriage or
contemplation of marriage, affecting all or any of the assets of the spouses in
a manner described in section 5;

The
FPA
further provides, in
sec. 5(1)
and
(2)

that:

Assets disposed of by agreement

5(1)        This
Act does not apply to any asset disposed of by a spousal agreement or
common-law relationship agreement or as to which the Act is made inapplicable
by the terms of a spousal agreement or common-law relationship agreement, but
where a spousal agreement or common-law relationship agreement is silent as to
an asset this Act if otherwise applicable to the asset applies as if the

inapplicable by agreement

a spousal agreement or common-law relationship agreement by its terms makes a

145
]

As a result,

146
]

The husband
says he did not know what was in the agreement and had no idea what the wife’s
assets were when he signed it.  He also says that the wife told him that if he
signed, she would not consider herself bound by the agreement.  For those
reasons, he asks the court to find that the agreement is not valid.

[
147
]

The wife says
that there were three drafts prepared.  She agrees with the husband that he
refused to read the first draft, in English only.  She then had it translated
to Hebrew and she says that when the husband read the Hebrew document, he said
he would not agree to a document which contained a commitment about giving the
Get

or Jewish divorce in the event of a separation.  She then had the provision
about the
Get
removed.  On giving him the revised document, she
suggested he see a lawyer and he refused, saying “I am a lawyer.”  She says she
told him that she needed to protect her family assets which had been gifted to
her.  He said he did not agree with a prenuptial agreement, but if that was
what she wanted he would sign it in Canada, before the wedding.

[
148
]

Both parties
agree that when they met with the rabbi who was to perform the wedding in order
to sign the document, he spoke to the husband about including a provision for
the
Get
and that the husband again refused.  The wife says the rabbi
went over each clause of the simple two-page agreement; the husband disagrees.
While the wife subpoenaed the rabbi, in the end, she did not call him as a
witness.  The husband located the two other witnesses to the agreement but,
some ten years later, neither recalled the event at all.

[
149
]

I do not
believe that the husband did not know what was in the agreement before he
signed it.  He knew it was a prenuptial agreement.  He knew that the wife’s
family was wealthy.  He knew that a family trust had purchased an expensive
house for them to live in and indeed, he had refused to make the mortgage
payments because they did not own the house.  Further, it seems entirely consistent
with his personality that he would reject a suggestion that he see a lawyer.
Even if I accept that the husband did not want to sign it, he has not advanced
any credible facts that suggest any type of coercion, duress or undue influence
that would render the agreement invalid.

[
150
]

The husband
also says that the wife did not provide full disclosure as he did not think the
wife had any property at the time of the marriage.  He was basically correct in
his assumption as all she “owned” was a discretionary interest as beneficiary
in a family trust, a trust she did not control in any way.

[
151
]

This interest,
whatever it was worth, would not have been shareable in any event as it was
acquired well in advance of the marriage.  Further, the funds advanced to the

inheritance, again, non-shareable assets.

152
]

In the result,
I find the wife’s version of events believable.  I accept that the husband was

153
]

Accordingly, I

FPA
.

SHAREABLE PROPERTY/MARITAL PROPERTY REFERENCE

[
154
]

The assets at
issue include the parties’ household effects, including wedding presents,
alleged cash of some $175,000, and the wife’s Israeli pension.

[
155
]

On separation,
the wife withdrew one-half of the parties’ joint bank account and the husband
kept the remainder.  There is nothing further to divide.

[
156
]

The husband
claims that he and the wife had about $175,000 in cash.  He seeks the division
of these funds which he says were given to the wife’s father to invest for the
couple.  He alleges that, in April 2002, the wife brought between $50,000 and

$115,000.  In evidence he differed at times about the exact amounts but says
this was their money and it was given to the wife’s father to invest for them.
The wife and her father deny this.

[
157
]

Given my
findings about the husband’s credibility, before determining whether these
funds exist, I must ask what objective evidence exists about them.

[
158
]

The husband’s
brother-in-law testified that, before the parties left Israel, the husband
asked him to keep a sealed manila envelope, about 8.5 x 11 for him until they
left for Canada.  There was some writing on the front of the envelope and he
saw the words “Charles Shore” and “$75,000.”

[
159
]

The husband
says that the envelope was full of cash, representing fees he received from
various clients over the years.  He says that the other $40,000 represented
money he had received from his father.

[
160
]

The husband
says the $40,000 was given to him by his father because the husband’s own
investment in about that amount had not matured.  He says the arrangement was
that his father would be repaid from those funds on their maturity date.  The
only independent evidence in support of this claim is tangential in that the
husband filed an undated letter from an Israeli bank which indicated that funds
in the name of the husband were paid out to his father under a power of
attorney in December 2004.

[
161
]

There is some
evidence that the husband did, as he says, legal work “on the side” and for
cash during the marriage.  However, in examining his work history and the
periods where he was unemployed and in receipt of unemployment insurance, I
find it improbable that he would have been able to amass either sum he alleges
was taken to Canada in 2002.

[
162
]

In assessing
the assertions of the husband, my findings on his credibility, the denials of
the wife and her father and the documents the husband presented, I find that
the husband’s evidence has not satisfied me on a balance of probabilities that
these funds existed.  Accordingly, this will not form part of an accounting
before the Master.

[
163
]

The husband
also claims one-half of the wedding presents received by the couple and half of
the household possessions.  When the parties came to Canada, they valued the
replacement cost of their personal property being shipped at $42,000.  On
separation the wife did give him some furniture which he later returned to
her.  She then sold the furniture at auction and kept the proceeds.  She admits
that she has all the wedding presents.  The division of this joint property is
referred to the Master.

[
164
]

The last asset
to be considered is the wife’s pension with her Israeli employer.  When the
parties moved to Canada, the wife continued working for the same employer,
albeit as an independent contractor.  The pension remained in existence until
sometime after separation when the wife ceased working for the Israeli company
and cashed it in.

[
165
]

The wife argues
that this pension is exempt from sharing because of the prenuptial agreement.
While I have found the agreement to meet the requirements of the
FPA
,
I do note the agreement is silent about the wife’s pension.  As a result, I do
not find that the agreement is specific enough to exclude the pension, given
the strict requirements set out in
The
Pension Benefits Act
,
R.S.M. 1987, c. P32, (“the
PBA”
) regarding opting out of a
pension plan.

[
166
]

The relevant
portions of the
PBA
are
Sec. 31(2)
and
Sec. 31(6)
as follows:

Division of pension benefits on
breakup

31(2)       Subject
to subsections  (3), (4), (6) and (8), where

(a) pursuant to an order of
the Court of Queen's Bench made under
The
Family Property Act
, family
assets of a person are required to be divided; or

, s. 19;

the pension benefit credit of the spouses or the parties, as the

]

interplay between these sections, I find that the parties’ prenuptial agreement
