SPOUSAL SUPPORT

[
168
]

The husband
claims spousal support.  He says he gave up a flourishing career in Israel and,
as a result of the move to Canada and the subsequent separation, has had to
begin anew in Canada.  The wife denies the husband was doing well in Israel.
She says the fact that he has not flourished in Canada is as a result of his
own personality problems and not related to the marriage or its breakdown.

[
169
]

Despite the
husband’s arguments that he had a good private practice while in receipt of
unemployment insurance, I find that the husband was not particularly successful
in the practice of law in Israel.  He had a number of jobs and was unemployed
for lengthy periods of time.  I do not accept the husband’s evidence that he
successfully practiced on a cash basis as there is little or no independent
evidence to support his assertions.  In my view, at least from January 2002 to
October 2002, the wife’s income was the main source of support for the family, with
the husband’s unemployment insurance income simply supplementing her earnings.

[
170
]

On arrival in
Canada, the husband was not permitted to work.  The wife had been able to
arrange to continue working for her Israeli employer and she was the sole
support to the husband and the children.  While friends and family suggested
that the husband take courses or do volunteer work while waiting for a work
permit, the husband refused to consider these options.  He understood, as part
of the agreement to move, that his father-in-law would find him a well-paying
position once he was able to work.

[
171
]

The marriage
ended less than five months after the return to Canada.  The husband was
devastated.  He had no work permit and so was unable to work.  His only source
of funds was one-half of the parties’ joint bank account, some $7,500.  The
wife expected the husband to live off this money until his work permit came
through.  The husband had an apartment, a borrowed car and cell phone which the
wife expected him to pay for.  He had few social supports and very limited
knowledge of Canadian customs and his environment outside of the wife’s milieu.

[
172
]

In my view, the
wife’s expectation that the husband should be able to “sink or swim” on his own
after separation was patently unreasonable.  Had there been a spousal support
application immediately post-separation, I have little doubt that the husband
would have been awarded some spousal support, at least on a short-term basis,
to provide him with the necessary resources to properly establish himself.
Instead, he was required to utilize his limited capital from the joint bank
account for living expenses.

[
173
]

However, the
husband’s behaviour with respect to becoming financially self sufficient since
then has been so problematic that the issue of support, some four years
post-separation, is not as clear.

[
174
]

The husband was
granted a work permit about six weeks post-separation but was not qualified to
practice law.  He attempted several part-time minimum wage jobs, but either
quit or was fired from each of them.

[
175
]

Prior to the
husband’s return to Israel in September 2003, he withdrew his application for
permanent residency in Canada.  He says it was because he needed the
application fee back, but it seems more likely that he thought it might help
him have the children returned to Israel via a
Hague Convention

application if the application was withdrawn.  When this avenue did not prove
possible, he decided to return to Canada on a permanent basis as the children
were clearly going to remain here.  However, as the wife had withdrawn her
sponsorship when the husband cancelled his application, he had to remain in
Israel until his reapplication to Canada was approved.

[
176
]

The husband
finally received approval and returned to Canada in June 2004.  However, he did
not get admitted to law school as a special student until September 2005.

[
177
]

He spent one
year at the law school and was asked to leave, apparently as his marks were not
satisfactory.  He supported himself by way of student loans during this year.
However, his marks are sufficient for the National Accreditation Committee to
permit him to write challenge exams in five other areas of law, provided he
does so within a certain timeframe.

[
178
]

However,
between April 2006 and May 2007, the husband has not pursued his studies
towards writing these exams, according to him, because he has been too
preoccupied with this trial.  He said that once the trial ended he would
continue his studies and hopes to be qualified to practice by, at the latest,
the summer of 2008.

[
179
]

In the meantime,
the husband is apparently being supported by his parents.  He has had several
other poorly paying jobs, from which he has either been fired or quit.

[
180
]

The wife says
that the husband’s inability to adjust to Canadian life, find a job and be
productive is a result of his own issues and do not relate to the marriage.

[
181
]

I reject her
submission.

[
182
]

Section 15
of
the
Divorce Act
gives direction to the court by setting out
certain factors and objectives in relation to spousal support as follows:

15.2(4)           In making an order under subsection
(1) or an interim order under subsection (2), the court shall take into
consideration the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of each
spouse, including

(a)      the length of time the spouses
cohabited;

(b)     the
functions performed by each spouse during cohabitation; and

(c)      any
order, agreement or arrangement relating to support of either spouse.

---

15.2(6)  An order made under subsection (1) or an
interim order under subsection (2) that provides for the support of a spouse
should

(a)      recognize
any economic advantages or disadvantages to the spouses arising from the
marriage or its breakdown;

(b)     apportion
between the spouses any financial consequences arising from the care of any
child of the marriage over and above any obligation for the support of any
child of the marriage;

(c)      relieve
any economic hardship of the spouses arising from the breakdown of the
marriage; and

(d)      in
so far as practicable, promote the economic self-sufficiency of each spouse
within a reasonable period of time.

[
183
]

In considering
these factors and objectives, I find that the husband has been economically
disadvantaged by the breakdown of the marriage.  The choice to uproot made by
the couple during the relationship has had serious economic consequences for
the husband in that on separation, he was unable to continue his profession,
was required to deplete his capital and leave the country once it was gone.  In
my view, I do not think that in the circumstances that existed at separation it
was in any way reasonable to expect that the husband should simply obtain
minimum wage employment as a way of moving on from the marriage.

[
184
]

If I consider
the wife’s alternate argument that he was never very successful as a lawyer, it
then becomes clear that she was supporting him, both in Israel and Canada.
While the marriage was not particularly lengthy, being some 7.5 years, at the
time of separation the husband suffered economic hardship in that he had no
ability to work at his chosen profession or establish his own household.  Both
in Israel and Canada the wife had provided him with all the necessities and
indeed many luxuries, including a nice home, a vehicle, the membership at the
Asper Campus, cell phones and the like.

[
185
]

Were it
immediately post separation, I would find that the husband was entitled to
transitional support to adjust to his new economic reality.  In these
circumstances, it seems to me that the husband should have had support for a
period of time to re-qualify as a lawyer.  He is required to pass exams in nine
practice areas.  He was able to pass four exams in one academic year and should
have completed the other five within the next year.

[
186
]

Instead, the
husband made some very poor choices and, four years post separation, is still
not qualified as a lawyer.  I find that his choice to engage in battle with
anyone he feels has slighted him has impeded him in becoming economically
self-sufficient and is not directly related to the marriage or its breakdown.

[
187
]

Had the husband
accepted the marriage breakdown, he could have enrolled at law school in the
academic year 2003-2004.  He could have met the requirements of the National
Committee on Accreditation by the spring of 2005. Had he not behaved in the
ways that he has, he would have been employable at the end of his studies and
the wife’s obligation to him would have terminated.

[
188
]

I find that the
husband is entitled to spousal support from the date of separation until April
30, 2005.  In determining this period of entitlement, I find that if the
husband had applied himself to becoming a lawyer here, he could have easily
done so in this time frame and that support of two years duration is
reasonable.

[
189
]

The wife
supplied me with calculations pursuant to the
Spousal Support Advisory
Guidelines: A Draft Proposal
, authored by Professor Carol Rogerson, Faculty
of Law, University of Toronto and Professor Rollie Thompson, Dalhousie Law School, in January 2005 (“SSAG”).  Based on these guidelines, the suggested
duration of spousal support ranges from 3.5 to 7 years which is a longer period
than I feel appropriate.  In these circumstances, given that the husband would
have tuition and book costs as well as living expenses, I prefer to make an
adjustment to the quantum of support to reflect this situation where the
support is for a retraining endeavour which would not have been necessary had
the parties separated in Israel.

QUANTUM

[
190
]

The issue of
quantum is a thorny one.  In considering the condition, means, needs and other
circumstances of the parties, I note firstly that the family lifestyle was
fairly lavish, as a result of the wife’s trust supplying them with a vehicle
and a large and expensive home in Israel.  With no shelter costs the family was
able to travel to Canada and elsewhere often, have a nanny for the children and
live a good life.

[
191
]

In examining
the wife’s present circumstances, her income is relatively modest, at least in
comparison to her lifestyle.  She earns approximately $48,000 per year from
employment and has income from her grandmother’s estate for a total income in
the $55,000 range.  She will receive a capital payment this year and another
one at age 40 from that estate.

[
192
]

During the
marriage, the wife entered into a transaction with the trust and her father in
order to buy the house in Israel.  Although the house was not owned by her, she
borrowed $365,000 from her father to pay down the mortgage the trust had taken
out.  Over the years, when she received funds from her grandmother’s estate and
elsewhere, she paid off the promissory note.  After separation, the trust was
wound down and the funds transferred to the wife.  As a result, she now lives
in a mortgage free, expensive house.

[
193
]

Even without a
mortgage on her home, the wife’s notional expenses exceed her income by a
significant amount.  The children attend private school, summer camps and do a
number of extracurricular activities, all paid for by the wife’s parents.
Without this help, the wife and children would not be able to live as they do.

[
194
]

She argues that
she has no ability to pay spousal support, particularly as the husband does not
contribute to the support of the children.  When I look at the wife’s expenses,
it is clear that her parents pay for most, if not all of the children’s costs.
I further note that the wife has not sought and does not want child support,
even if I impute income to the husband or he earns it in future.

[
195
]

As well as the
duration calculations, the wife supplied me with quantum calculations pursuant
to the SSAG which took into account that the payor of the spousal support was
the custodial parent.  These calculations attempt to take into account the
factors to be considered in making an award of support and the objectives of a
spousal support order.

[
196
]

Based on the
parties’ present income realities, according to the SSAG the range of spousal
support would be between $327 and $430 per month.  At the low end, the wife and
children would have 90.5% of the family income; at the high end it would be
87.93%.

[
197
]

The
calculations supplied take into account the economic consequences arising from
the care of the children.  Here, the wife is the sole support of the children
as a result of the husband’s choices and the high percentage allocation of
family income to the wife and children reflect that fact.

[
198
]

However, the
SSAG calculations intertwine the issues of range of support and duration. As I
have found a shorter duration than the SSAG recommends to be appropriate, I
find that the suggested monthly range is lower than it should be in these
circumstances.

[
199
]

When I look at
the husband’s circumstances at the time of separation, his major priority
should have been to pass the law exams so he could reestablish himself.
Besides his basic living expenses, he would have tuition and book costs. While
he attended law school, he was eligible for and received a student loan which
would ease his cash flow, but has to be repaid.  If he worked during the
summer, I expect that he would have earned enough to cover the book and tuition
costs.

[
200
]

At the end of
the marriage, the husband was left with virtually no assets and no ability to
practice his profession.  Since separation, the wife has moved from rented
accommodations to a $400,000 home.  Her ability to earn an income continues
unabated.

[
201
]

In my view, a
clean break is preferable for these parties and I find that a higher quantum
for a shorter period will more quickly bring the finality the wife wishes.

[
202
]

Taking into
account the criteria set out in the
Divorce Act

and the SSAG I
find that the appropriate amount of spousal support is $700 per month for a two
year period, payable through Maintenance Enforcement.  The support will
commence August 1, 2007 and the wife’s obligation to pay support will cease
July 31, 2009.  If the wife wishes she may “pre-pay” her monthly obligation in
one lump sum.

DIVORCE:
REASONABLENESS OF THE CHILD SUPPORT ARRANGEMENTS

[
203
]

The wife seeks
a divorce.  The grounds were proven at trial.  However, she sought no child
support.

[
204
]

Section 11
(1)
(b) of the
Divorce Act
states:

11. (1) In a divorce proceeding, it is
the duty of the court

(b) to satisfy itself that reasonable
arrangements have been made for the support of any children of the marriage,
having regard to the applicable guidelines, and, if such arrangements have not
been made, to stay the granting of the divorce until such arrangements are
made;

[
205
]

I must
therefore be convinced that the child support arrangements are reasonable
before I can grant the divorce.

[
206
]

At present, the
husband has no income.  As a result of his actions since separation, his
prospects are poor.  I am satisfied that he is not capable of earning an income
at least until he passes his exams.  I am further satisfied that he is
indirectly contributing to the support of the children through the reduced
spousal support award which leaves the lion’s share of the family income in the
hands of the wife and children.  I find the present arrangements for child
support reasonable.  I therefore grant the divorce, effective 31 days from
today.

[
207
]

However, if the
husband’s income situation improves in future, I see no reason why he should
not be contributing to his children’s support, despite the wife’s stated wish
to receive nothing from him on their behalf.  He will therefore provide the
wife with a copy of his income tax return on an annual basis, no later than
June 30
th
of each year, commencing June 30, 2008.

COSTS: SOLICITOR/CLIENT OR PARTY AND PARTY

[
208
]

The wife claims
costs and asks the court to award them on a solicitor and client basis.  The
husband’s first position is that each party should bear his or her own costs,
but alternatively, will ask for costs if the wife does.

[
209
]

The relevant
portions of Queen’s Bench Rule 57 are:

Factors in
discretion

57.01(1)    In
exercising its discretion under
section 96
of
The

Court of Queen's Bench Act
, to award costs, the court may consider,
in addition to the result in the proceeding and any offer to settle made in
writing,

(a)   the amount claimed and the
amount recovered in the proceeding;

(b)   the complexity of the
proceeding;

(c)   the importance of the
issues;

(d)   the conduct of any party
which tended to shorten or lengthen unnecessarily the duration of the
proceeding;

(e)   whether any step in the
proceeding was improper, vexatious or unnecessary;

(f)   a party's denial or refusal
to admit anything which should have been admitted;

(g)   whether it is appropriate
to award any costs or more than one set of costs where there are several
parties with identical interests who are unnecessarily represented by more than
one counsel; and

(h)

any other
matter relevant to the question of costs.

Costs against
successful party

57.01(2)    The
fact that a party is successful in a proceeding or a step in a proceeding does
not prevent the court from awarding costs against the party in a proper case.

---

Authority of court

57.01(6)    Nothing
in this Rule affects the authority of the court,

(a)   to award or refuse costs in
respect of a particular issue or part of a proceeding;

(b)   to award a percentage of
assessed costs or award assessed costs up to or from a particular stage of a
proceeding; or

(c)   to award all or part of the
costs on a lawyer and client basis.

[
210
]

In considering
whether costs should be awarded and to whom, the first step is to determine
which party had the most success.  In this case there were some thirteen
issues.  In my view, an analysis of my decision against the positions taken by
the parties can only lead to the conclusion that even though the husband had
success on some issues, on balance, the wife was the more successful litigant.

[
211
]

Accordingly, I
find that the wife is entitled to costs. I turn first to her claim for
solicitor and client costs.  She argues that the husband’s conduct of the
litigation was so atrocious that she should be fully recompensed for her out of
pocket costs, estimated to be somewhere around $150,000.  She says that he
extended and delayed the proceedings by virtue of calling useless witnesses,
lengthy and unproductive cross-examinations, and by his disrespectful behaviour
in the courtroom.  She argues that with an award of solicitor and client costs
the court would be expressing its extreme displeasure with the husband’s
conduct of the litigation and that ability to pay is irrelevant to the question
of whether to award costs of this kind.

[
212
]

The case law is
clear that an award of solicitor and client costs is an exceptional matter.
Ordering costs on this basis should be reserved for the most extreme cases:
McMurachy
et al v. Red River Valley Mutual Insurance Co.
(1994),
1994 CanLII 10984 (MB CA)
, 92 Man. R. (2d)
225 (Man.C.A.).

[
213
]

Further, in
determining whether an award of this kind is warranted the court must examine
factors such as consideration of a party’s conduct and the lack of merit in a
position before the court:
Hunter v. Hunter
(2000),
2000 MBCA 134 (CanLII)
, 150 Man.R.
(2d) 291;
230 W.A.C. 291
.

[
214
]

In this case,
there is no doubt that the husband often behaved in an outrageous manner.  He
did prolong the trial by calling some witnesses who had very little to add to
his case.  However, his position on many of the issues did have some merit,
even though he may not have achieved the success he hoped for.  I further make
some allowance for the fact that the husband, although legally trained in
Israel, was acting on his own behalf.

[
215
]

In the result,
I am not prepared to order costs on a solicitor and client basis.  While I
agree that the court should condemn the husband’s inappropriate conduct through
a costs award, I prefer to do so by relying particularly heavily on Rule
57.01(1)(d) in assessing costs on a party and party basis.

[
216
]

I find that the
husband’s conduct lengthened unnecessarily the duration of the proceeding.
However, I note that the wife took 24 days to put in her case and, as she was
determined to establish her case on access issues through, as described by her
counsel, a “pattern of past conduct”, this forced the husband to cross examine
on areas which were not particularly relevant to the issues I had to decide.
The husband (save for one witness called out of order) completed his case in 11
days and each side had 1 day for argument.  However, most of the husband’s
witnesses were not necessary as their evidence was not relevant to the issues
before me.

[
217
]

I find that
those extraneous witnesses added about 5 days to the length of the trial.
Further, I find that the husband prolonged the trial throughout by virtue of
his behavioural issues, particularly in his cross examination of the home
assessor which took almost 4 days.

[
218
]

As I indicated
during the course of argument, this is a Class IV matter on the tariff.  In
order to adjust for the husband’s conduct, I will allow double the fee allowed
for counsel for 7 days of the hearing.

[
219
]

As counsel did
not prepare a draft bill of costs, there may be other cost items to be spoken
to once it is complete, but the bill of costs I envision will, as well as
allowing for the trial, include all court matters leading up to the trial where
costs were not dealt with at the time of that matter.  I further find that
there should be an allowance for second counsel, given the complexity of the
matter, and those costs will be doubled for 7 of the days of trial as well.
